coherence.reasons: Both run diagnosis, then rejection of the labor cut, then levers, then sequencing. X's governing thought (fix gross margin and delivery, four quick moves protect the covenant, full plan reaches 3.0%) is carried through each layer: bridge, option table, lever sizing net of headwinds, FY2026 in-year bridge, capital and risks. It has small internal wrinkles: the three-store exit appears as +2.2 and +1.9 net, and the slide 15 title says $3.0M against a $2.5M net gain. Y's pyramid is clean and shorter, but its top-line claim of 'six actions reach 3.1%' sits beside its own note that the 2027 wage step would cost $7.3M against $1.5M of headroom. Its claim that the first three actions clear the covenant uses full run-rate values in year one. Those undercut the consistency between Y's headline and its evidence.

judgment.reasons: X weighs four options (management plan, defend on price, margin-led plan, delivery exit as fallback) against the covenant, FY2028 margin, one-time cost and the owner constraint. It splits levers into six data-backed (2.5%) and three negotiated (to 3.0%), and admits 3.0% has no cushion, with pre-agreed contingencies. It handles the trade-offs explicitly: promotional cuts carry a 15% volume-loss assumption and a ValuMart guardrail; labor is rebalanced (−3% in high-hours stores, ring-fenced fresh and receiving tasks) rather than cut; the three long-lease exits are deferred to a vote after two quarters because of a 3.4–4.1 year payback. Y's recommendation points the same way and is defensible, but its alternatives are mostly the draft plan and store-exit variants. It takes the full $10.5M promotional reversal with no volume loss and only 'hold their key prices' for ValuMart. It asks for all nine exits now because they are needed to hit 3.0%. And the plan reaches the target only by leaving out the known 2027 wage rise.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: margin bridge (labor 13%), gross-margin drivers (−0.70, −0.50, +0.18), e-commerce drag of −$10.4M, the 6.1% rebuttal, store exits of $6.6M and the fee test. X goes further: a wage versus productivity decomposition, an e-commerce model reconciled to Table 1 in every year, per-order economics for delivery versus click-and-collect, and a shrink risk range of $5–10M labelled as correlation. It also rebuts the category team's claim with numbers (1.6 points of comps pays for only 2.3 points of promo share), sizes levers on a post-closure sales base, phases FY2026 capture and runs sensitivities. Its weaknesses are team-estimated one-time costs (flagged), an ambitious shrink target of 2.2%, and a slightly over-read claim that promotions 'did not protect' ValuMart stores. Y's weaknesses are larger: the $10.5M promotional gain assumes no lost volume; shrink falls to the best-quartile level with no mechanism for where the hours come from; the plan total leaves out the 4% wage step in the pack; the covenant claim of $33M assumes immediate full run-rate; one-time costs are only the $7.5M lease exit. Y's treatment of lost online sales at 30% is arguably the more careful one, and it does note its shrink figure is an upper bound.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage-inflation hypothesis: labor is 13% of the decline, productivity absorbed most of the wage rise, the 8% cut feeds shrink, and the freeze locks in the e-commerce loss. X tests the draft plan through the same model to FY2026 and FY2028 ($19–24M against the covenant, 0.9–1.2% margin). It keeps the parts that hold up: wages still matter through the 2027 step, so it adds targeted scheduling, and it keeps the freeze for home delivery only. It also shows its own 'margin only' starting hypothesis failing at 1.8% and being extended. Y revises cleanly with a side-by-side against the draft plan, but it simply cancels the labor action and leaves the forward wage pressure outside the plan, so its update is less complete.

overall.reasons: Both reach a defensible R1-type conclusion on a correct quantified bridge, and Y is commendably concise. X would serve the CEO and board better on three counts. Its plan adds up to 3.0% after the known wage and delivery-rate headwinds. It gives a credible phased FY2026 covenant bridge (about $24M) rather than a full run-rate claim. And it covers second-order effects, a capital budget inside the $25M envelope, sensitivities, contingencies and clear board decisions. Y's headline 3.1% and $33M covenant figure would not survive lender or board scrutiny once the 2027 wage step, promotional volume loss and ramp-up timing are applied.
